name: Frequency Non Profits
note: Finds local nonprofits that gather volunteers and supporters in person, and drafts one note each. Draft only. Ships off.

offer.pitch: A page, calendar and supporter list for a local nonprofit, with no cut taken of what supporters give.

niches.label: Community, arts, youth and neighborhood nonprofits

angles.line: The people who show up for you are in four different lists.
A volunteer comes to one day and never hears about the next.
Event and donation tools take a cut of what supporters give.

niches.label: Environmental, garden, food and service groups

angles.line: A volunteer comes to one cleanup and never hears about the next.
Filling a volunteer day takes more than one post.
Volunteers, donors and members live in separate lists.

hunts.link_line: If you'd like a free page for your organization on Frequency, start here:

playbook.seek: Who to find: local nonprofits and community organizations in the region that gather people in person: arts and culture groups, community gardens, beach and trail cleanups, food shares, youth and mentoring programs, neighborhood associations, friends-of-the-library and friends-of-the-park groups. Keep one only when a public page shows a volunteer day, a community event, a class or a regular meeting people can come to.
playbook.signals: Strong signs, best first: a volunteer or events calendar with something in the next 60 days; a recurring volunteer day with its own name; sign-ups handled through a general form or ticket site; a named volunteer coordinator or program lead with a listed email; a local chapter page that runs its own events. Weak signs: a donate button and nothing to come to.
playbook.where: Where to look: the organization's own website and its volunteer, events and get-involved pages, city and library community calendars, local volunteer listings, and event pages on Eventbrite and Meetup.
playbook.queries: Searches that work: "<town> volunteer day", "<town> beach cleanup", "<town> community garden volunteer", "<town> friends of the library", "<town> arts nonprofit events", "<town> food share volunteer", "<town> neighborhood association meeting". Use each area's own town names.
playbook.skip: Skip national charities' head offices, political campaigns and parties, hospitals and universities, grant-making foundations with no events, and anything that is only a fundraiser appeal.
playbook.rank: Order leads.json best first, because only the first few are kept: a local group with a named recurring volunteer day and a coordinator's listed email comes first, then one with an events page and a contact form, then the rest. One lead per organization, addressed to the person who runs it when the page names them.
playbook.record: In leads.json the event is what people can come to: event.title is its name or what kind of thing it is, event.url is the public page that shows it, and starts_at may be empty. The organizer is the nonprofit, with the coordinator's name when the page gives it.
playbook.note: Write a short, warm, personal note to each one. Name the work they do or the thing people can come to loosely and say what you like about it; never give a date, time, price or address, and never mention money, donations or how many people came. End that opening with an exclamation mark. Then, in a new paragraph, say: "I'm Daniel, founder of Frequency, a free way for neighbors to find local, in-person gatherings and the people who hold them." and ask one easy question that fits them, such as whether they would like their volunteer days where neighbors can find them.

hunts.name: Nonprofits that gather people
hunts.looking_for: Local nonprofits in North County San Diego with a public volunteer day, community event or regular meeting
